Heretick
HER-e-tik
n. (a factious man; one who divides the church by choosing his own opinion)
From Greek hairetikos, from haireomai, to choose — a man who takes his own party. The Authorized Version spells it with the -ck and uses it once, in Paul's instruction to Titus.

Biblical Definition

A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject. The instruction is a procedure, not an outburst, and the two admonitions are the heart of it. The man is warned, warned again, and only then rejected, and Paul explains why the rejection is warranted at that point: knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself. The self-condemnation is the diagnostic. After two plain warnings, a man who persists is no longer mistaken but choosing. The context is a chapter about avoiding what is unprofitable: but avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. The Greek word behind heretick is about faction and self-chosen party as much as about doctrinal error; the two usually travel together, which is why Paul also says heresies are among the works of the flesh, beside variance, emulations, wrath, and strife. And Corinthians states the strange providence in it: for there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who holds to a heresy; one who maintains an opinion repugnant to the established faith; in Scripture, a factious man to be rejected after two admonitions.

expand to see more

HERETIC, n. A person under any religion, but particularly the christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.

HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.

SCHISM, n. In church affairs, a division or separation; a breach of unity among people of the same religious faith.

ADMONITION, n. Gentle reproof; counseling against a fault; instruction in duties; caution; direction.

EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of the faithful.

Key Scripture

Tit 3:10 — "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;"

Tit 3:11 — "Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself."

Tit 3:9 — "But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain."

1Co 11:19 — "For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you."

Modern Corruption

The word is used either as a weapon against anyone who disagrees about anything, or retired entirely on the ground that no one may be excluded; Paul's instruction has two warnings before it, a specific diagnosis, and a defined end.

expand to see more

Two abuses of Titus 3:10 are equally common. The first skips the admonitions, applying the label to a first disagreement and treating every difference as a fundamental one. Scripture's own practice is more patient: Paul withstood Peter to the face over a real error and did not reject him; Apollos was taken aside and taught the way of God more perfectly; the weak brother in Romans 14 is to be received, not disputed with. The word is reserved for the man who has been warned twice and persists in dividing.

The second abuse retires the category altogether, on the view that exclusion is always unloving. That reading has to discard a great deal: mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them. A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house. Church discipline is commanded, its purpose is restorative — that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus — and a church that cannot say no eventually cannot say anything.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hairetikos (G141), factious, heretical; hairesis (G139), a choosing, a party, a sect; ekstrepho (G1612), to turn inside out, to subvert.

expand to see more

Greek hairetikos (G141) — factious, given to party spirit; the one occurrence, Titus 3:10.

Greek hairesis (G139) — a choosing, a sect, a party; there must be also heresies among you.

Greek nouthesia (G3559) — admonition, warning; after the first and second admonition.

Greek ekstrepho (G1612) — to turn out, to pervert, to subvert; he that is such is subverted.

Greek autokatakritos (G843) — self-condemned; being condemned of himself.

Usage

"“after the first and second admonition reject” — the single occurrence."

"“being condemned of himself” — the diagnosis that warrants it."

"“avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions” — the surrounding counsel."
